detailHeading: Why fences lean in Georgian Bay country
detailBody: Most leaning fences start at the posts. Each winter, wet soil around Collingwood freezes and expands, which lifts posts set too shallow. After a few freeze-thaw cycles, the post tilts and the panels pull with it.

Rot is the other common cause. Posts sit in damp soil season after season, and the wood breaks down at grade, where you cannot see it. A post that wobbles when you push it is often rotted at the base, even if the top looks fine.

Fixing a few posts and boards often extends the life of a fence that is otherwise sound. If most posts are soft or boards are failing along the whole run, the service provider can confirm whether replacing a section makes more sense than patching it.

faqs.q: Can new boards match the existing fence?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Note the board width, profile and spacing in your request, with a close photo. New wood looks lighter at first, so stain or sealer on the repair helps it blend over time.

faqs.q: Is repair or replacement the better choice?
faqs.a: If the posts are mostly solid and the damage is limited to a few boards, a gate or one section, repair is often the practical choice. If many posts are rotted, replacing the run can make more sense. The service provider can confirm which fits.

faqs.q: How can new posts resist rot?
faqs.a: Posts rated for ground contact, set in concrete shaped to shed water, with the top of the footing above grade, stay drier where rot usually starts. Ask about the post method when you talk through scope.

faqs.q: Can a gate that drags or will not latch be fixed?
faqs.a: Often, yes. A sagging gate usually starts at the hinge post. A repair can include squaring the frame, adding bracing and replacing worn hinges or latches so the gate closes properly.

faqs.q: Can the request be for a cottage fence?
faqs.a: Yes. Note the property address, how to access it and whether you will be there. The service provider can confirm coverage and plan around access.

detailHeading: Why drywall patches show, and how to avoid it
detailBody: Most patches show for three reasons. The compound goes on too thick, the edges are not feathered wide enough, or the repair is painted without primer. Bare compound takes paint differently from the wall around it, so the patch shows as a dull or shiny spot.

A repair built up in thin coats, sanded between coats and primed before paint is less likely to show. On textured walls and ceilings, the texture needs to match first so the patch reads the same under side light from a window.

Water stains need more care. In Collingwood homes and lakeside cottages, ceiling stains often come from ice dams, roof leaks or a slow drip under a bathroom. The source has to be fixed first. If the drywall stays soft or shows mould, that section usually needs replacing instead of paint.

faqs.q: Can a patch match the existing wall texture?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Common textures like orange peel and knockdown can be matched, and smooth finishes are feathered and sanded. Include a close photo taken with side light so the texture shows.

faqs.q: Can the repaired area be painted too?
faqs.a: Yes, a request can include priming and painting. Painting the full wall, corner to corner, usually gives the most even result, especially if the existing paint is older. Include the paint name if you have it.

faqs.q: What if there is mould behind water-damaged drywall?
faqs.a: Removing the damaged section shows the cavity. Small areas of surface mould on framing are cleaned and dried. Widespread mould needs a remediation specialist before new drywall goes up, and the service provider can confirm what applies.

faqs.q: Should the leak be fixed before the drywall?
faqs.a: Yes, the leak needs to stop first. If you are not sure where the water came from, say so in your request. Where the source involves plumbing, a licensed contractor may be required, and the service provider can confirm what applies.

faqs.q: Can drywall be repaired in a rental or before a sale?
faqs.a: Yes. Requests often cover holes and wear between tenants or before a listing, along with touch-up painting so the rooms are clean and ready to show.

detailHeading: When a renovation needs a general contractor
detailBody: A single repair rarely needs a general contractor. A kitchen, bathroom or basement project usually does, because the work involves several trades in a set order. Plumbing and electrical rough-in come before insulation and drywall. Drywall comes before tile, trim and paint. When that order slips, finished work gets torn out.

A general contractor plans that sequence up front and keeps the project on track. Carpentry and finishing are often handled directly, while licensed trades take on the work they are required to do, such as electrical and gas.

For cottages around Georgian Bay, coordination matters even more. Owners are often away, so regular updates and the right people on site at the right stage help. Work that needs a licensed trade should be identified before anything starts.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a handyman and a general contractor?
faqs.a: A handyman takes on individual repairs and smaller jobs. A general contractor manages a whole project, including the order of work and the trades involved. Describe your project and the service provider can confirm which fits.

faqs.q: What size of project fits this request?
faqs.a: Small and mid-size renovations, such as kitchens, bathrooms, basements and multi-room updates in homes and cottages. Describe the project and the service provider can confirm if it is a good fit.

detailHeading: Choosing flooring for Georgian Bay homes and cottages
detailBody: Humidity around Georgian Bay swings widely from summer to winter. Solid wood moves the most with those changes, which is why engineered hardwood and vinyl plank are popular here. Both handle seasonal swings better. If your cottage sits unheated in winter, check the product’s temperature rating before you buy.

For entries, kitchens, basements and cottage living areas, vinyl plank is a practical pick. It resists water and handles sand and grit well. Laminate suits bedrooms and living rooms but should stay out of areas that get wet.
A floor is only as good as what is under it. The subfloor needs checking for squeaks, soft spots and dips before installation, and some products need time to acclimate before they go down.

faqs.q: What flooring works best for a cottage?
faqs.a: Vinyl plank is a common choice for cottages because it resists water and handles sand and grit. If the cottage is unheated in winter, check that the product is rated for those temperatures. The service provider can talk through options before you buy.

faqs.q: Can flooring you already bought be installed?
faqs.a: Yes. Note the product name in your request and have the boxes on site. The service provider can check the installation requirements and plan the underlay, trim and transitions.

faqs.q: Can new flooring go over the existing floor?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Vinyl plank and laminate can go over some flat, solid floors, but not over carpet or soft, uneven surfaces. Floor height at doors and appliances also matters. The service provider can check the existing floor and confirm whether removal is needed.

faqs.q: Does the furniture need to be moved first?
faqs.a: It helps to clear small items, electronics and anything fragile. Mention larger furniture in your request so the plan covers who moves what and where it goes.

faqs.q: Why is subfloor preparation so important?
faqs.a: Most flooring problems start below the floor. Dips cause click joints to separate, high spots cause rocking, and loose panels cause squeaks. Fixing the subfloor first keeps a new floor flat and quiet.

detailBody: Many small problems around a Collingwood home get worse with each season. A door that sticks in August and swings freely in January tells you the frame or hinges have shifted. Worn weatherstripping lets in cold air and moisture. A loose railing only gets looser.

Grouping repairs into one list makes sense. Several items can often fit into one visit, and one quote can cover the lot. Keep a running note on your phone of anything that sticks, squeaks, drips or rattles.

Some fixes point to a bigger issue. A door that keeps binding can mean settling, and a stain near a window can mean a failed seal. Mention anything like this in your request so the service provider can review it.

detailBody: Kitchen cabinets get more handling than any wall in your house. Grease from cooking, hand oils and cleaning sprays all work against paint. A finish that looks good on day one can chip at the edges if the prep is rushed.

Prep matters most. Doors and drawer fronts come off and get labelled, and every surface is degreased before sanding. A bonding primer goes on next, then cabinet-grade paint in thin coats. Doors go back up once the paint has cured enough to handle use.

Most solid wood and MDF cabinets paint well. Oak grain shows through paint unless it is filled first, so mention it if you want a smooth look. Thermofoil and laminate doors that are peeling need a different approach, and the service provider can confirm if replacement is the better option.

faqs.q: Will painted cabinets hold up to daily use?
faqs.a: With proper prep and the right products, yes. Degreasing, sanding and a bonding primer give the paint something to grip. Cabinet-grade paint cures to a hard finish that stands up to cleaning and regular handling.

faqs.q: Can all cabinets be painted?
faqs.a: Most wood and MDF cabinets paint well. Laminate and thermofoil can be painted in some cases with special primers, but peeling thermofoil is not a good candidate. Include photos of your cabinets and the service provider can confirm what will work.

faqs.q: Will the wood grain show through the paint?
faqs.a: Open-grain woods like oak show texture through paint. If you want a smooth, modern finish, the grain can be filled before priming. Mention the look you want in your request.

faqs.q: Can the kitchen be used while the cabinets are painted?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. The cabinet boxes are painted in place and the doors are painted away from the kitchen. Plan to empty the cabinets being painted and keep counters clear while the work is underway.

faqs.q: Is this a good time to replace hardware?
faqs.a: It is a good time to do it. New handles and knobs finish the look, and old holes can be filled if the new hardware uses a different spacing. Include your hardware choice in the request if you have one.

Keeping the sink, range and appliances where they are keeps the work simpler and the budget easier to manage. Moving them means new plumbing, gas or electrical runs, which may require licensed trades. The service provider can walk you through what each change involves.

In cottages and older homes around Collingwood, floors are often out of level and walls are rarely straight. Both need checking before new cabinets go in, so the cabinets can be shimmed and scribed to sit level and tight to the wall.

detailHeading: When a fixture swap needs a licensed plumber
detailBody: A fixture swap connects a new faucet, toilet or sink to supply and drain lines already in the same spot. The water is shut off, the old fixture comes out, and the new one goes in with fresh supply lines and seals before every joint is tested.
Moving a sink, adding a fixture where there was none, or running new supply or drain lines is different. That work may require a licensed plumber, and the service provider can confirm what applies.

Older homes and cottages around Collingwood often have seized shut-off valves, corroded supply lines or mismatched fittings. These need checking first, so you know if a valve or line needs replacing along with the fixture. If a cottage was closed for winter, mention it, since lines and fixtures may need a check after a freeze.

faqs.q: Can a fixture you already bought be installed?
faqs.a: Yes. Have it on site and check the box for the parts list. Some fixtures need a specific supply line or adapter, and the service provider can confirm that when reviewing your request.

faqs.q: Does replacing a faucet or toilet need a plumber?
faqs.a: A straight swap on existing supply and drain lines is a common handyman job. For new supply or drain runs, moved fixtures and larger plumbing changes, a licensed contractor may be required, and the service provider can confirm what applies.

faqs.q: What if the shut-off valve will not close?
faqs.a: Old valves often seize or drip once they are turned. A faulty shut-off valve can be replaced as part of the fixture swap, so you have water control at that fixture.

faqs.q: Can older cottage plumbing be worked on?
faqs.a: Yes, within the scope of a fixture swap. The valves, supply lines and drain connections need checking first. If the older plumbing needs more than a swap, a licensed contractor may be required, and the service provider can confirm what applies.

faqs.q: Is help available to choose a fixture?
faqs.a: Yes. The service provider can confirm what fits your existing sink, counter and connections, such as the faucet hole count or toilet rough-in size, so the fixture you buy suits the space.

detailHeading: Pressure washing after a Georgian Bay winter
detailBody: Winters around Collingwood leave road salt on driveways and garage floors, and damp shade near Georgian Bay feeds moss, mildew and green algae on siding, decks and north-facing walls. Left in place, algae keeps surfaces slippery and holds moisture against wood.

More pressure is not always better. High pressure can etch soft wood, scar composite, strip joint sand from interlock and push water behind siding. The pressure, nozzle and cleaner should suit each surface, with a soft wash on siding.

Spring and early summer are popular times to wash, once the risk of frost has passed. If you plan to stain a deck or fence, wash it first and let the wood dry fully before staining. A request can cover the cleaning and the stain or sealer as one job.

faqs.q: Is pressure washing safe for all surfaces?
faqs.a: Not at full pressure. Soft wood, composite, older mortar and siding all need gentler methods. Adjusting pressure and nozzles for each surface, with a low-pressure soft wash on siding, helps avoid damage and water getting behind the panels.

faqs.q: When is the best time to pressure wash?
faqs.a: Spring and early summer work well around Collingwood, after the last frost, once salt and winter grime have built up. Washing in fall before closing a cottage also helps keep mildew from setting in over winter.

faqs.q: Are cleaning solutions used?
faqs.a: For mildew, algae and heavy staining, the surface is often pre-treated with a cleaner suited to the material, with plants wetted down and landscaping protected. Plain water is enough for many jobs.

faqs.q: Should a deck be pressure washed before staining?
faqs.a: Yes. Stain needs a clean, dry surface to soak in and bond. Washing removes dirt, mildew and loose grey fibres. Let the wood dry fully before staining. A request can include both the washing and the staining.

faqs.q: How often should a property be washed?
faqs.a: Many homes and cottages need it once a year, often in spring. Shaded areas near trees or water can need it more often. The service provider can confirm which surfaces need regular attention.

detailHeading: A maintenance rhythm for Collingwood homes and cottages
detailBody: Freeze-thaw cycles, heavy snow and lake humidity are hard on buildings around Georgian Bay. Caulking cracks, gutters fill with leaves and needles, and exterior wood takes on moisture. Many expensive repairs start as small issues no one had time to catch.

Spring and fall are the two key visits. In spring, check for winter damage, clear gutters and look at decks, railings and caulking. In fall, clear gutters again after the leaves drop, change furnace filters and seal gaps before the cold sets in.

For cottages and seasonal homes, regular visits matter more because no one is there to notice a problem. A set task list helps, with any needed repairs noted and checked with you before work goes beyond the plan.

faqs.q: What is included in a seasonal maintenance visit?
faqs.a: That depends on your property. A typical visit covers gutters, caulking, weatherstripping, filters, alarm batteries and a walk-around for damage. The task list is built with you, and any repairs found are noted for your approval.

faqs.q: How often should maintenance be scheduled?
faqs.a: Most homes do well with a spring and fall visit. Cottages, rentals and properties with more upkeep may need visits more often. The service provider can suggest a schedule based on the property and how it is used.

faqs.q: Can the request cover a cottage or seasonal home?
faqs.a: Yes. Regular upkeep can be combined with cottage opening and closing. Note how to access the property and anything you want checked while you are away.

faqs.q: Can landlords and property managers send a request?
faqs.a: Yes. Requests can cover routine upkeep and small repairs for rental properties. For several units or ongoing work, see the property manager maintenance page or list your properties in the request.

faqs.q: What if a task needs a licensed trade?
faqs.a: It gets noted and raised with you. For work that needs an electrician, plumber or gas technician, a licensed contractor may be required, and the service provider can confirm what applies before any of it goes ahead.
